title: Old Man Brown's advice to read the audience
summary: Wooding recalls the songs sung and Brown's lesson to watch the crowd and play what suits its mood.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: But do you remember what kind of songs they were singing? Were they singing sweet songs? The girls?

Well, they sang all kinds of songs. There was a song they called 'Shimme-Sha-Wobble'. And there was a song called, "I Wish I could Shimmy Like My Sister Kate". And then there was songs called, "I Lost You, So Why Should I Care". And then, we had the others, you know, different types of songs, and that's one thing Old Man Brown told me, too, he said -- and I never forgot it. Later on, I told a little lady working with me, Rae Harrison, I told her the same thing. He said, "Sam, don't set up on that piano and play like a gawk. Turn around and look at your

audience and see what condition they're in. Now, if you see a lot of people sitting around there like they're moonstruck or something like that, what are you going to play the "Strutters' Ball" for, what are you going to play like that? You want to go into something like, "I Lost You, So Why Should I Care", or something like that." You know what I mean?
Now, if they come in there lively, you don't want to play, "I Lost You, So Why Should I Care", or , "The Rosary".

You've got to watch your audience and see what they want. And you'll catch them at a different time, and you might they come in there and want, "Toot, Toot, Tootsie, Goodbye". You've got an audience like that, you want to give them how they feel. And I've found that that can be used today. A lot of times, a lot of people use the wrong things on the wrong people at the time.
